title: RBI Swap Facility Draws $40.8 Billion in Foreign Inflows as Rupee Defence Gathers Steam
excerpt: Foreign currency deposits account for the bulk of inflows under the central bank's concessional hedging programme, with SBI Research projecting up to $85 billion by year-end.
body:
• The Reserve Bank of India's concessional swap facility has attracted $40.81 billion in foreign currency inflows since its June launch, according to data released on August 1.
  • FCNR(B) deposits contributed $36.7 billion — the largest share — while ECBs and OFCBs added $4.07 billion combined.
  • SBI Research projects total inflows of $80–85 billion by the time both windows close, with FCNR deposits alone potentially reaching $65–70 billion.
  • The facility offers banks zero-cost hedging on three- to five-year foreign currency deposits, making India an attractive destination for NRI and institutional capital.

The Numbers So Far

India's central bank has pulled in $40.81 billion through its special foreign exchange measures launched in June, the RBI said in data released on Saturday. The bulk — $36.7 billion — came through Foreign Currency Non-Resident deposits raised by banks under a zero-cost hedging window that runs through September 30.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=B3LDXjyFLrc

External Commercial Borrowings contributed $1.5 billion, while Overseas Foreign Currency Borrowings added $2.57 billion, according to Reuters. The ECB and OFCB window remains open until December 31.

"The concessional swap facility has seen avid interest and attracted steady forex inflows since June 8, 2026."

— Reserve Bank of India press release

How the Facility Works

The RBI introduced the dollar-rupee swap facility on June 5 and operationalised it three days later, as part of a broader package to shore up India's balance of payments during a period of elevated crude oil prices and persistent equity outflows. Under the scheme, banks can swap fresh FCNR(B) deposits with the RBI at par — exchanging dollars for rupees today and reversing the transaction at the same rate at maturity — effectively eliminating hedging costs.

The facility accepts deposits in any freely convertible currency but offers swaps only in US dollars. Underlying deposits carry a one-year lock-in period, and the swap cannot be cancelled once executed.

Why It Matters for NRIs

FCNR(B) deposits are fixed-term foreign currency deposits available to non-resident Indians, persons of Indian origin, and overseas citizens of India. Because they are denominated in foreign currency, depositors bear no exchange-rate risk, and both principal and interest are fully repatriable. The RBI's zero-cost hedge has made these deposits significantly more attractive to banks, which can now offer competitive rates without absorbing currency risk.

The pace of inflows has been striking. SBI Research estimated that FCNR(B) deposits reached $26–28 billion by July 23 — just 45 days into the programme — surpassing the roughly $26 billion mobilised during the 2013 special FCNR(B) window, which took nearly three months.

The Bigger Picture

The swap facility is one piece of a broader defence. The government has also exempted overseas investors from capital gains tax on government bonds, opened new long-dated bonds to foreign buyers, and relaxed concentration limits on short-term foreign investment in debt. Analysts at HDFC Bank estimated the combined measures could bridge a $40–50 billion gap on India's balance of payments for FY27. Jefferies has been more bullish, projecting $50–70 billion in total inflows.

SBI Research's latest projection is the most optimistic yet: $65–70 billion in FCNR deposits alone, with total inflows from all three schemes potentially reaching $80–85 billion.

What to Watch

The FCNR(B) window closes on September 30 and the swap facility on October 16. The ECB and OFCB windows run through year-end. How much of the projected pipeline converts to actual deposits in the remaining two months will determine whether the RBI's gambit fully offsets the pressures that prompted it.
nri_angle: NRI depositors benefit directly from zero-cost hedging on FCNR deposits, making India a more attractive destination for overseas savings.
